utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll conclude the evidence of General today, so leave at the end at least 20 minutes or half an hour for the Prosecution for its re-direct examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: May I just very briefly introduce Ms. Jovana Paredes, who is assisting me today and is one of my legal assistants and will be here throughout the afternoon. I have to bow out after the session and Ms. Vukajlovic will be taking my place. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber was so informed. Thank you for the introduction. Welcome. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. We will do our best to finish the most important things we have to deal with with Sir Michael Rose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, do you agree that in 1984 [as interpreted] after the incidents with NATO, the attitude of Serb soldiers and civilian authorities remained correct and fair nevertheless towards the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recall is that the Bosnian Serb side became increasingly difficult after the summer of 1994, and in no way complied with the agreement for full and free movement of convoys. Sir, could I have the screen on the left with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Our usher will help you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your book on page 161, you confirm that the Bosnian Serbs had not intended to take Gorazde. That is also confirmed by that conversation of mine that Mladic recorded in his diary, that we had taken more than we had intended to and that our objective was to make it impossible for attacks from -- to take place from Gorazde. Now I'm referring to the difficulties between UNPROFOR and the Serb army -- or rather, the Serb side after the bombing in Gorazde. Do you agree that despite the reasons and irrespective of the reasons in the crisis involved, the attitude towards your soldiers remained fair and correct, nevertheless?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not agree there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us see now what you stated in your statement of the 24th of May, 1995, on page 7. 1044-297 is the ERN number: [In English] "As a result of the air-strikes, UN troops were detained for symbolic rather than malicious reasons" -- [Interpretation] And it says that you were not concerned about their safety. Here's the statement: [In English] "Those UN troops were detained for symbolic rather than malicious reasons during times" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the General can orient himself, that's also contained at paragraph 90 of his written evidence that has been submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Very kind of you, Ms. Edgerton. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "During the times of Karadzic, the BSA computer overloaded and froze. It took times to re-boot the system. I was never worried at any stage of the personal safety of each detainee but so that this whole process could unveil the peace process and success to date. We still remained partial and had not been defeated by General Mladic because we were not at war with him."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, yesterday you said that your bombing, or rather, the NATO bombing at your request was not full scale, rather, it was symbolic. And then you say that the Serb army responded to that symbolic bombing by symbolically keeping the soldiers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your last quote, your last sentence should read: "We still remained impartial," instead of "partial." Continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [In English] "We still remained impartial." [Interpretation] That's what I read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, in your view, this was a symbolic bombing and the response, in your view, again was symbolically detaining UN troops. Is that not your very own sentence?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never used the word "symbolic," to the best of my memory relating to the air-strikes by NATO. I was accused many times in the media of only using pin-prick attacks, not strategic-level bombing. But I didn't use the word "symbolic" myself. With regards to the paragraph you've just read out, that's what I felt at the time, that the Bosnian Serb side had an interest in maintaining the presence of UNPROFOR in that country. Their own people, 600.000 of them, were being fed by the United Nations' aid. And therefore, although they presumably felt they had to be seen to be doing something in response to the air-strikes against them by NATO, which involved the taking of hostages, I did not think in the long term those hostages would come to any harm. And, indeed, they were usually released soon after they were taken without any harm or without any detriment to their equipment or themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I simplified matters when I said that the bombing was symbolic, but you had certainly said that that level of bombing would not have turned you into our enemies. And that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- 7575 is the 65 ter number I'd like to have now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, because of overlapping, your answer to the accused's statement was not recorded. Could you repeat it kindly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I was replying that -- my reply was: That was correct, replying to the point made by Dr. Karadzic, that the level of bombing did not turn us into the enemies of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not it -- oh, yes, it is. This is probably the translation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska reporting to myself and to the chief of Main Staff and the commands of all corps on the 17th of April, that is to say a week after the bombing in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 3. I believe it should be page 3 in English as well. It is paragraph 3, the situation in the territory. It's the last page actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the first week of our discontent, discontent with the bombing that is. This is what the General Staff and General Milovanovic are saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the last page, paragraph 3. Now we have the transcript. Can we have that same document but just the last page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you bear with us. The usher's computer has some technical difficulty. It will be coming soon. So while we are waiting for the document, you can put your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, as you will see, paragraph 3 says that General Milovanovic is reporting to the effect that the army had visited all of these UNPROFOR and UN personnel to see how they were being treated, and the conclusion was that their treatment was excellent and fair and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 4 in English, paragraph 3, the first sentence refers to that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you recall that there was a blockade of UNPROFOR and the military observers in the Ilijas Brigade? Do you remember why that happened -- or rather, first of all, do you remember that the Army of Republika Srpska visited all of your soldiers and was assured that they were all well?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were in the hands of the Bosnian Serb army, so it was not surprising they were being visited. They should not have been taken hostage in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the difference is a conceptual one. We did not think that this was a minor bombing; we thought that this was a major bombing, but never mind. Look at paragraph 3, there was this crisis with regard to the Ilijas Brigade. We remembered that during the interview, too. Do you recall that there was this misunderstanding in relation to Cekrcici, was it within the 20-kilometre zone or not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember there was some debate, but the details of that I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you did confirm that in your view the centre of the exclusion zone, that circle, was by the circle in Marin Dvor, remember?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the first epicentre of the 20-kilometre circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at paragraph 4 now, at 1600 hours -- or actually 1610. A message was intercepted that aircraft are expected in the area of Gorazde after 1700 hours. Do you agree, General, that the Serb army was under terrible pressure due to this possible bombing and that it significantly affected our relations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was inevitable that the bombing was going to have a detrimental effect on the relationships between the UNPROFOR and the Bosnian Serb side. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D706, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, we're dealing with Gorazde now and we'll go on. 6852 is the 65 ter number I'd like to have now. Do you remember the demilitarised zone of 3 kilometres, do you remember the establishment of that zone that ended this crisis around Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that I had accepted that, I had even proposed it and agreed upon it with Mr. Akashi?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that matches with the facts as I recall them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please cast a glance at this. This is a telegram from General de Lapresle to Mr. Akashi. It's on the 21st of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the second page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, we see here that this pertains to that part of the exclusion zone that is to the east of the Drina River. This relates to the agreement that was signed by Milovanovic and Delic on some other piece of paper; however, you were there in the capacity of a witness. We can see that down here, can we not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, yes. I signed as a witness, but I notice that General Delic hadn't signed it because I think we took the document on to General Delic after this. And whether he signed it or not, I can't remember. I suspect he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, that is a fact. However, there used to be this custom of the Serb and the Muslim side signing the same document on different copies, though. However, you do recall that Delic didn't want to sign it at all. Look at 3: [In English] "The BiH commander commits himself not to undertake any offensive action. The only armed personnel in the shaded area on the attached map will be those of UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] Do you recall, General, that it was only the Serb side that was demilitarised, only the Serb side of that zone, that is to say the Serb villages on the eastern bank of the river?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 4 so that the participants can cast a glance at the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the map attached to this agreement, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the shaded area, is it under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I guess there was nothing within the 3-kilometre circle that was by then under Serb control because they had withdrawn their troops from that circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, did they withdraw from this shaded territory? Before the withdrawal was this Serb-held territory?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it probably was, although the exact details of the final positions I cannot remember. But it looks as though that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, General, that the unshaded part of the circle that was under the control of the Muslim army had not been demilitarised in any way?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true to say I think that the Bosnian Serb forces did not demilitarise in that 3-kilometre circle, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Bosnian Serb forces or Bosnian --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnian state forces, the national forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Bosnian state forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank You, Excellency. This is exactly what I wanted to ask for a clarification. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document has been admitted as Exhibit P1664.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D2549 is the next document. Can we also have the English version. I'm sure we have it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, General, sir, that this is a report on a conversation between General Van Baal and General Milovanovic which took place on the 22nd of May, 1994? Maybe I can draw your attention to the heading. This is an intercept which was taken by the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, State Security Service. In other words, the secret service of the Muslim part of Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly I can't comment on this document with any accuracy and I don't think I can make a contribution in terms of advancing the knowledge of this Court. But it sounds as though that sort of conversation could have taken place. Certainly it's an incomplete version, I suspect, of what happened. But the person obviously to ask is General Van Baal if he appears as a witness. He was one-half of that conversation; I was not. What is certain is that the Bosnian Serb side did not withdraw all their forces from the 3-kilometre circle to start with, but dressed them either as civilians or as policemen and kept them in the zone. And only after pressure from UNPROFOR were they finally withdrawn - the date I can't remember. And I think that is reflected in this intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This document is of three pages. Would you like to see them all before --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be helpful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Why don't we let General go through them. We can collapse the B/C/S for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you agree with me, you can see that Milovanovic is surprised because the Serbs and UNPROFOR had signed at the highest level and the Muslims didn't. And here it is requested even from the policemen to leave after the heavy weaponry had left. So we were requested to do even more than we subscribed to, and the Muslims on the other hand did not have to do anything at all. Do you see what Milovanovic says: [In English] "I have nothing to add for the moment. When the Muslims put their signature to that document I will react that very moment immediately. I cannot establish a cease-fire unilaterally before that time, before the document is signed by the Muslim side. While we establish the cease-fire from our side, the Muslims opened fire ..." [Interpretation] And so on. Do you agree with me that in this case, as in many other cases, the Muslim side tried to gain an advantage from our mutual agreements?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we discussed previously, Dr. Karadzic, the status of the Bosnian state forces were differently from those of the Bosnian Serb forces, in that the Bosnian state was recognised by the United Nations as a member state and therefore they had every right to keep their armed forces on their sovereign territory, whether it was an enclave or not. And I guess that's why General Delic refused to sign that document. It would have been helpful if he had done so and they had withdrawn their forces from the perspective of peacekeeping, but obviously their national considerations of sovereignty persuaded them otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, who was it who told you and when that the Serb side was not an equal party to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never informed in those terms, but it was evident and self-evident from the United Nations Security Council Resolutions which had recognised the state of Bosnia. Indeed at the time I seem to remember we were not permitted to use the two words "Republika Srpska," in case we gave an informal recognition to that entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, General, sir, we were Bosnians as well. We constituted the majority of the power and over 60 per cent of the territory. Never mind that. Some of our misunderstandings may have originated from the understanding that the Bosnian government was legitimate and that the Bosnian state was legitimate, whereas on the other hand the Serbs were not legitimate; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that may well have been the case, yes. There were two very different positions there: That of the Bosnian Serbs and that of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then it becomes much clearer why we suffered as we did and why we had so many misunderstandings. General, sir, you see that you are wrong and finally we did get the status of an equal side. We will have another witness who will talk about that in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can the Court please produce 1D2537. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, can I draw your attention to the title: [In English] "Protocol Additional to the Geneva Conventions of 12th of August, 1949 ..." [Interpretation] Now let's look at paragraphs 1 and 3. In paragraph 1 it says: "It is prohibited for the parties to the conflict to extend their military operations to zones on which they have conferred by agreement the status of demilitarised zone, if such extension is contrary to the terms of this agreement." And now paragraph 3: [In English] "The subject of such an agreement shall normally be any zone which fulfils the following conditions: "(a) all combatants as well as mobile weapons and mobile military equipment must have been evacuated: "(b) no hostile use shall be made of fixed military installations or establishments: "(c) no acts of hostility shall be committed by the authorities or by the population: And: "(d) any activity linked to the military effort must have been ceased." [Interpretation] I'm sure that you knew all of that, General; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was certainly aware of The Hague protocols and the Geneva Convention, but not in any great detail. I was working at the time from the United Nations Security Council Resolutions relating to the safe areas, and those were 824 and 836 which did not call on the Bosnian government forces to demilitarise those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, this was implied in our agreements that we signed for Zepa and Srebrenica, and they refused to sign anything else; right? Only the borders of Zepa and Srebrenica were defined and the Muslim side never subscribed to any agreements about any other protected areas; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, this was before my time. I inherited a situation in 1994 which I could read about and indeed could talk about with my interpreter who was present at the time, but whatever information I may contribute now would be second-hand and not valuable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you were briefed about what you were going to inherit, and you inherited only agreements about Zepa and Srebrenica; you did not inherit any other agreements because there were none?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly knew of the agreement relating to Srebrenica and Zepa, but I was by then conforming to the requirements of the Security Council Resolution 824 and 836 which in a way had superseded what may or may not have been agreed by General Morillon and General Mladic at the time. Certainly the Bosnian government forces did not demilitarise and hand in other than useless weapons in the case of Srebrenica. That was the situation I'd inherited.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the next page, please. Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, there is a maxim from the Roman law, lex specialis derogat lege generalis, are you saying that Security Council Resolution could derogate the protocols of the Geneva Conventions or did it have to comply and conform with those conventions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Security Council Resolution was passed, those two resolutions were passed in response to a particular set of circumstances on the ground and may not have related precisely to the terms of the Geneva Protocols or The Hague Convention -- the Geneva Convention or The Hague Protocols or whichever way around that is expressed. This was a specific set of resolutions to deal with a specific matter, and the conditions that prevailed on the ground may not have been within the orbit of the protocols and conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they legal or political documents in that case?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me questions, Dr. Karadzic, I'm not competent to answer. I merely know that I was applying the two resolutions there, 824 and 836, with regards to the antecedence and whether they were conforming or not to the conventions and protocols of The Hague and Geneva is something that an international lawyer would have to make judgement on, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since the sanctions were applied, the resolutions had to be legal rather than political documents. If sanctions were applied and if air-strikes were applied based on a political act, then the world is going in a very wrong direction. In any case, General, could you please look at bullet point 7: [In English] "If one of the Parties to the conflict commits a material breach of the provisions of paragraphs 3 or 6, the other Party shall be released from its obligations under the agreement conferring upon the zone the status of demilitarised zone. In such an eventuality, the zone loses its status but shall continue to enjoy the protection provided by the other provisions of this Protocol and the other rules of international law applicable to the armed conflict." [Interpretation] Party that violates an agreement also deals -- does away with the status of a protected zone. Wouldn't that be the interpretation of this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I can't make any comment on the legal aspects of the Security Council Resolutions that I was supporting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the General hasn't come to testify as an expert in legal matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it is necessary to admit this kind of legal document. We can refer to the protocols of Geneva Conventions at any time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, in regard to His Excellency Judge Kwon's intervention, let me be clear what direction I can take from now on. Yesterday you said you can't talk about the political aspects of the crisis; today we hear that you're not familiar with the legal aspects of the whole matter. Will you agree with me that we should reduce your testimony in terms of legal and political implications and merely stick to the facts?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think your presumptions are probably wrong. I mean, it would be helpful just to stick to facts, I agree; but your presumption that I wasn't aware or refused to discuss political or legal aspects is not right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, not only is it not right, but numerous questions you asked and the General answered pertain to matters which were both political and military, and indeed as a result of that had legal elements to them. So your presumption is not only not right, it's patently wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I will have to go through the transcript of the examination-in-chief because there the first part of the sentence is usually correct because it pertains to facts and the second part of the sentence contains political views. That's why I'm suggesting that we should reduce the testimony, but if we can't do that then I shall continue, I shall proceed. P984 is an exhibit that has been admitted. Can we see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, these are the resolutions -- actually, this is Resolution 824.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the second page. We don't need the Serbian version unless the interpreters need it. Can we go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please look at paragraph 3: [In English] "Declares that the capital city of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sarajevo, and other such threatened areas, in particular the towns of Tuzla, Zepa, Gorazde, Bihac, as well as Srebrenica, and their surroundings should be treated as safe areas by all the parties concerned and should be free from armed attacks and from any other hostile acts ..." [Interpretation] Do you agree with me that this pertains to both sides or would you say that this pertains only to the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite clearly it pertains to both sides because it uses the word "all parties concerned."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This has been admitted, so I don't have to -- thank you. Here in your book on page 139 in e-court you say: [In English] "While we contemplated our next move, Churkin called from Pale with the news that the Serbs were prepared to help the fighting withdraw to a distance of 3 kilometres from the centre of town, establish a 20-kilometre total exclusion zone around Gorazde, and release all the hostages. They also wished to return to the conference table and re-start the peace process. This was extraordinary news coming as it did at the moment of complete collapse of -- by their adversaries." [Interpretation] And then the next paragraph: [In English] "When we conveyed the news of the Serb offer to the Presidency, Izetbegovic and Salajdzic accused Akashi of having failed in his mission." [Interpretation] When Serbs offered peace, Salajdzic and Izetbegovic were angry and they were angry because fighting had not continued; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why they were angry or not I can't say. My impression at the time is that they were angry because the United Nations refused to call for heavier air-strikes by NATO than the United Nations thought appropriate. Both President Izetbegovic and Prime Minister Salajdzic expected at that point NATO to bring about the military defeat of the Bosnian Serbs by bombing, and that's something which the United Nations wouldn't sign up to. That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Correct. You are saying that the extraordinary news was met with anger in the Bosnian Presidency. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will tender this for admission once we tendered the whole book. And now 1D110, can we have that. 1D00110, 110. Thank you. This is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the document which was issued on the 1st of June, 1994, after all of our talks, after the 3-kilometre zone was defined as well as the exclusion zone of 20 kilometres. And now Enver Hadzihasanovic, the minister of defence, writes to the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We will see that on the second page. He says: "In the desire to launch activities in order to alleviate the situation in the Drina valley and to create the necessary preconditions for the long-term resolution to this complex problem, we hereby propose under 1: "Urgently implement the organisation of the 8th Corps, involve units in Srebrenica, Zepa, and the OG Pazaric." And then there are staff proposals, who the commanders are going to be. And then at the bottom it says: "The appointed commander should lead a group of officers to Gorazde and a unit that would have to consist of at least 200 well-equipped soldiers."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Bullet point 4: "Major financial assistance should be approved and they should be taught to use UNPROFOR as suppliers. "A special helicopter transport should be organised to deliver materiel and technical equipment especially for anti-armour combat." General, sir, Alija Izetbegovic at the bottom writes: "I agree for the most with everything including bullet point 2." Do you agree that these preparations and activities on the part of our Muslim adversaries were not in agreement with our efforts to implement the agreement on demilitarisation and the exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously the attempt by the Bosnian state forces to re-arm and re-equip their troops in Gorazde, particularly if they had a subsequent intention of opening up combat operations, again was unhelpful to the peace process. That's absolutely true. But I think an awful lot of that is wishful thinking on the part of the Bosnian state forces because of course there's no way that the UN helicopters were ever going to carry military equipment for them. And indeed on one occasion when we discovered they were trying to smuggle satellite communications, we destroyed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can see under 4 they are hoping that they will train men in Gorazde to use UNPROFOR for supplies. I'm again saying and I'm not asserting that the higher commands were aware of that, but Muslims certainly knew that the troops in Gorazde should be trained, should be thought how to get closer to UNPROFOR troops and how to get supplies. Would you have been cross had you seen this in your day during your tour?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, any attempt by the troops of the warring parties to use UN equipment or use their positions to prosecute further their war would, of course, be something we would not have accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this increased Serbian suspicions about those links between the Muslim troops and UNPROFOR troops at lower levels, that this increased our suspicions and level of caution on our side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really make any useful comment on what motivated the Bosnian Serb side any more than I can what motivated the Bosnian government side, other than supposition on our part. Because, as I say, we were not in a position to gather intelligence about what your motivations may have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm just trying to make a distinction between certain things. I'm trying to see whether the Serbs were genuinely against the United Nations, or were they actually right to harbour suspicions and fear, as the Secretary-General of the United Nations said? Because the Muslim side drew benefits from their co-operation with the UN. This is important to demonstrate the motives on the side of the Serbs, were the Serbs against UNPROFOR or was there just an attempt to fight against the Muslims? I'm sure that you would have been angry if you'd seen this, but let me tell you the Serbs were angry as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think you exhausted that issue. Move on to your next question and refrain from making a speech.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D707.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's one document you didn't tender, it is the intercept we saw before. You are not minded to tender that, intercept between Mr. Van Baal and Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly. It's going to be easier when Van Baal comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll leave it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, even if the Muslim had not demilitarised their part of the circle, 3 kilometres, and we did have to demilitarised, do you agree that it is impermissible for them to further reinforce those 3 kilometres of theirs with such actions, reinforcements by way of equipment and personnel? What were the Serbs supposed to do, were they just supposed to watch all of that happening?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about a hypothetical situation, which is again, as I say, not useful to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, certainly you would understand that we have the right to defend ourselves if they attack us, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't answer a question like that yes or no without knowing the circumstances in which you were being attacked. If you had launched - and I'm talking hypothetically - an attack against Gorazde, the enclave, and the Bosnian state forces had responded, that would be legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if they attack us from Gorazde, is our defence encounter an offensive legitimate?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The view of the United Nations at the time was that we were trying to bring about a peaceful settlement to the conflict and that we regretted any attack that was made against side against another, particularly when civilian casualties were the result of those attacks, or because of the increased level of conflict it was impossible to deliver humanitarian aid to the people who needed it. We condemned all attacks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2476, could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, General, that was no response to my question. Does that mean that governments have the right to beat their citizens and to kill an entire ethnic community just because they are recognised as such, although we are an unavoidable part of that government, that state, as a matter of fact. Were the United Nations tolerating Muslim attacks against us and on the other hand they were not tolerant of us and were highly critical of us?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first part of your question is straying into international law again, which I already said I'm not competent to comment upon; the second part I've already answered. We condemned all attacks, particularly when civilian communities were being endangered by those attacks. We were working, particularly in 1994, the middle of 1994, a period you're discussing at the moment, with the hopes to bringing about a permanent cessation of hostilities in Bosnia during that time. And it is a matter of great regret that the possibilities for peace that were worked so hard for by the United Nations were abandoned by both parties to the conflict at the beginning of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If this is it, can we have -- oh, I'm not sure this is it -- oh, yes, it is, yes, yes. Can we have the next page, please. General, sir, may I draw your attention to this telegram of yours, forwarding General Mladic's letter to UNPROFOR, the command in Sarajevo, and to you as commander and your associates, because we see that this is in the plural, it says "gentlemen." General Mladic is informing you in this letter that: "... according to the regulations of the Geneva Convention of 1949" and the additional protocols we saw a few moments ago there cannot be any military installations or important industrial plants or factories, and so on and so forth, in safe areas. He is informing you of the fact that there is an ammunition factory in Gorazde called Pobeda and that it is within the 3-kilometre zone. Also that there are many people who are employed there and that the power-supply ensured by the UN, by way of generators, is used to manufacture ammunition. That is what the first paragraph says. Can you see that yourself?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can see the allegation, but of course I don't agree with it in any way at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the factory called Pobeda exist in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There certainly was an old ammunition factory there; whether it was operating or not, I have no idea at all. I very much doubt it, given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Old or not old, General, it manufactured brand new ammunition. If you were not aware of that, your colleague General Mladic informed you about that, that that was the case; and that those generators they had been asking you for are generators they do not use for civilians, but rather for manufacturing ammunition that is to be used against us. That is quite clear from this letter and in the third paragraph he asks you to deal with this urgently and to take efficient indispensable measures to resolve the situation. Do you recall this letter? And on the basis of this letter, did you check whether the factory was actually operating?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure General Mladic received an appropriate reply from Mr. Akashi. I actually can't remember receiving this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D708.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, what I am trying to say to you here and to all the participants is that whenever the suspicions of the Serb army proved to be true -- I mean, we did not mind having generators brought in to help civilians. But if generators are used in order to have this kind of factory operate in a safe area that is supposed to be demilitarised and Mladic ascertained that, don't you understand that our objections and our restrictions were not on account of the UN but on account of abusing the UN, that is to say that is what our adversaries did. Don't you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN would never have permitted its humanitarian aid to be used to further the military effort no matter whether it was helping with generators or in any other form. Aid was aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could they have been doing that without your permission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The United Nations deployments to Gorazde were not in the form of an army of occupation where we were able to go around and make searches. It's possible, of course, they were running their factories and making their ammunition, but as I said I think it's extremely unlikely. It's equally possible that when we gave you fuel to clear the roads on the Bosnian Serb side for the delivery of humanitarian aid, some of that fuel went to your tanks or artillery and some of it went to running your own routes for military purposes not for humanitarian aid. But as I say, we don't know whether that was the case. The allegations were frequently made by the Bosnian government that the fuel we had given you was used for that. So it becomes fruitless getting involved and I'm merely giving this as an example of bandying accusations backwards and forwards when the United Nations were working in extremely difficult circumstances trying to bring about a cessation of hostilities, meanwhile supplying aid to the people of that country, 600.000 of whom were Serbs. We acted in an impartial and proper manner, and to suggest otherwise is to make the sacrifices of those people who died during the United Nations peacekeeping mission unworthy, and that is not the right thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. For your information, we gave Croats electricity for crude oil. There were 600.000 Serbs in Croatia. All right. That's just something that I'd like you to know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D258.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in Croatia there were 600.000 Serbs and in Bosnia about 1.5 or 1.6 million?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess that was roughly the population distribution, yes. Of course it was very difficult to know what the population distribution was after the start of the war. That may have been the case at the start of the war, but it probably wasn't the case by the time I got there in 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, that's not this document. 1D2518. Perhaps I misspoke a moment ago, 1D2518.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we are turning to the situation around Bihac, General. This document pertains to Bihac. Do you agree or do you recall, rather, that the Muslim 5th Corps carried out a major offensive against the Serbs out of Bihac, out of Bihac which was a safe area, they attacked the Serb populated areas in Krajina? You do know that, don't you? It's not written here, but I mean I'm asking you whether you remember that. First of all, do you remember that the 5th Corps had almost reached Bosanski Petrovac and that they seized vast parts of the territory there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember precisely the sequence of events, although I remember the fighting around Gorazde extremely well. And I don't -- am not quite sure where this document comes from and what its status is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the United States government and it is permissible to use it in this court. Number 1 reads: [In English] "UN official blames Muslims for Bihac clashes."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Alan Roberts, UN protection forces spokesman for Sector South said at today's regular news conference in Knin that the present clashes in the Bihac region are a consequence of attacks launched by the Muslim army's 5th Corps on Serb positions in the areas of Bosanska Otoka and Bosanska Krupa. Therefore, Roberts said this does not constitute an act of aggression on the part of Republika Srpska army. Alan Roberts denied information that members of the Serb army of Krajina have been shelling Bihac." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. We can all read this, can we not. General, don't you see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's an excerpt from "Tanjug" report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it is an excerpt from a "Tanjug" report related to a conference that is authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember this. Sorry, I can't remember this document and I certainly can't remember the incident or the press conference referred to. I suspect that it came from Croatia press conference, not from the Bosnian press conference because I don't think Roberts was one of mine. I think he worked for the Croatian UN mission, not from the Bosnian UN mission. Knin was outside of my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, look at the next paragraph. On the right it says: [In English] "UNPROFOR spokesman Claire Grimes ruled out UN military action to help the fighting in Bihac pocket." [Interpretation] Two paragraphs down: [In English] "Fighting is concentrated on the confrontation line. It is not targeting Bihac town which is the safe area." [Interpretation] And two paragraphs further down: [In English] "On Saturday, UN Bosnia commander, Lieutenant-General Sir Michael Rose warned the Serbs to halt their attack on Bihac town or face action by the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation." [Interpretation] Well, General, sir, when the units of the 5th Corps advanced towards Banja Luka capturing large portions of Serb territory, torching Serb villages, no one threatened them. How could they accuse you of being a pro-Serb officer when you never threatened them, only us. Look at this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But don't you remember what it says here that you threatened the Serbs to stop otherwise that you would call in NATO?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that very well. I thought you were referring to why I was being called pro-Serb. As I say, I don't have any reply to that, but I can reply that I do remember indeed warning the Bosnian Serb forces not to continue their attack on the town of Bihac. That is correct. Whatever may have pervade that attack of course was not saying which the UN had become involved in at that point. What we did become involved in was the attack against the safe area of Bihac. There were many battles going on around Bosnia which we had no knowledge of during 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember your warning issued to the Muslims not to leave Bihac and not to attack the Serbs? Was there any warning of that kind?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would certainly have stated our reservations about the launching of attacks from the safe areas to the Presidency, and I'm sure we did that on many an occasion. Our correspondence with General Dudakovic on the ground was patchy to say the least, he being in command of the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it possible, General, that the Muslim side had misinformed you to the effect that we are bombing the town? We were actually legitimately in pursuit of the 5th Corps, whereas they are misinforming you that we were attacking the city. Was this possible or plausible?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly possible that they had attacked out of Bihac with the 5th Corps against our warnings and that you had counter-attacked and were -- had driven them back into Bihac and were now involved in shelling Bihac. That is probably what happened, but that didn't prevent our -- us from exercising our responsibility towards deterring attacks against safe areas, warning you to desist and to cease those shelling attacks. And that's why we called in NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no objection from you, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D709.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, some UN representatives confirmed here that certain national battalions had an unprincipled stance, a biassed one, in favour of one particular side, specifically the Muslim side. Does your knowledge correspond to that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. We had accusations from both sides. The Bosnian government side continually accused the Russians of siding with the Serbs and they -- vice versa, you accused the Muslim forces within the United Nations of siding with the Bosnia government side. It was an argument we were used to and got rather bored with by the middle of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D2517, please. 1D2517.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, let us have a look at this letter that was sent to you, or rather, to Ambassador Akashi, de Lapresle, and you yourself. You see here that General Milovanovic is complaining to you, saying that the Bangladesh Battalion is interfering in the war on the Muslim side, they're arming the Muslims and providing them with information that they gather as they gain insight into our situation. Do you remember that crisis with regard to the interference of the Bangladesh Battalion? Do you remember that this offensive of the 5th Corps took place after the Bangladesh Battalion arrived in Bihac?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly remember the fighting in Bihac happening whilst the Bangladesh Battalion was there, but I refute any allegation that they were supporting the Bosnian state side. They were lightly equipped, very lightly equipped, battalion. The weather wasn't particularly good, and I doubt if they'd had any capability in terms of being able to assist the Bosnian government forces even if they'd wished to. I certainly had no reports from the military observers there on the ground of anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that because of these suspicions and these reports, you transferred them from the Bihac pocket to Pleso, the Zagreb airport or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that certainly didn't happen in my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the last paragraph: [In English] "With respect to the aforementioned, we request that you urgently apply pressure on the Muslims in order that they both cease offensive activities, in particular those against civilian settlements, and withdraw to the positions as they were on 23rd of October, 1994. Otherwise, we will be compelled to retaliate towards the area we have been attacked from." [Interpretation] General Milovanovic is quite legitimately providing information to the effect that we have been attacked and that a UN battalion or the Bangladesh Battalion is interfering and that if you do not stop them from attacking Serb territories we would react ourselves. Do you recall this letter?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you do anything in relation to this request of General Milovanovic's?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've explained, Dr. Karadzic, we spent an enormous amount of time trying to reduce the level of conflict when there were letters like this received. We certainly would have taken the allegation up with the Bosnian government side, and if we had had evidence that they were launching assaults, we would have counselled them strongly not to say to do in the midst of what was supposed to be a peace process. That happened in June and it happened subsequently in and around Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. But they could fully envisage what would happen if we would launch a counter-offensive. You would attack them with sharp words and us with sharp bombs; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose you could put it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this document admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D710, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would this be the right time for the break or do we have another ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for 25 minutes. We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have any of the documents been unadmitted? No. Can the Court please produce 1D2536.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you remember that during that crisis and during any crisis there was an intense correspondence between yourselves and us, between your generals and our generals, between me, Akashi, and de Lapresle and so on and so forth. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This one of the letters dated 17 November, my letter to General de Lapresle and the UNMO at Pale forwarded that letter. Could you please cast a glance at the letter and the letter was written at the peak of the crisis. In this letter, do I inform General de Lapresle that I understand his concern but also do I point to the fact that our counter-offensive was preceded by a major offensive by the Muslim forces against us and that we believed that UNPROFOR is responsible for the current events because -- [In English] "We simply cannot allow the Muslims to create a strong hold in 'safe areas' and use them as spring boards for staging attacks against us under the cover of UN and NATO. A 'safe area' is presumably supposed to benefit civilians, it is not supposed to be bristling with armed soldiers." [Interpretation] And further on I continue to say: [In English] "It is not our intention to make the civilians in the Bihac pocket suffer. We are merely exercising our legitimate right to self-defense, and we shall be pursuing every armed Muslim. If this means entering the 'safe area' in order to disarm the Muslims, then so be it. Given the fact that UNPROFOR did not or could not demilitarise the pocket, it seems that we have to do it ourselves. But I wish to assure you that unarmed civilians or, for that matter, UNPROFOR positions in that area, are certainly not our target." [Interpretation] Is this a legitimate position, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly not a position that I would agree with because I don't believe you should be attacking into the safe areas no matter what the provocations may be. We were trying to bring about peace at that time in any offensive and whatever excuse was regrettable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a while ago I asked you whether you allow for the possibility that you were disinformed by the Muslim government. We were pursuing the 5th Corps and they informed you that we were actually attacking the town; right? Was that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that is your position, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D711, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you didn't know about any manipulations or disinformation or misinformation, or perhaps you did know that they misinformed you and that's how they provoked NATO into acting against us; which is true?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only actions taken by NATO as a result of requests by the United Nations came about from direct observation by the United Nations military observers on the ground. We did not respond to the Bosnian government's request for air-strikes against the Bosnian Serbs on any occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question was this: Is it possible that you did not receive proper information, that you were misinformed? If you think that you have answered, then we can move on. Let me repeat: Is it possible that you were misinformed? Is it possible that the Muslim government fed you erroneous information?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were being fed erroneous information by all parties to the conflict, but that did not necessarily mean we acted upon this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2520, can the Court produce the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it, does Colonel Daniell ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. He was my Chief of Staff in the second half of my time in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is his unclassified fax message to the main UNPROFOR staff in Zagreb dated 25 November 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you confirm that this is a fax that was sent on the 24th of -- 25th of November?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I correct something I said. He was my military assistant not my Chief of Staff during the second period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, this fax describes the contents of your meetings with the Serbian and Muslim sides. The Serb side was represented by Koljevic, Tolimir, and Zametica; the Muslim side was represented by Salajdzic, Muratovic; and on your side, Rose, Andreev, and Gobillard. Let's look at paragraph 4: [In English] "Two points to note: A, Heavy disinformation throughout the meeting about the shelling of Bihac and Serb attacks. Subsequently proved false, the BiH are firing heavy weapons out of the town centre and now (1630) we learn that the Serbs are responding. Many calls from Ganic to attack with air-strikes. It is possible that the meeting has been arranged to buy time to allow the Serbs to attack Bihac the darkness tonight." [Interpretation] And can we go on to the following page where it says: [In English] "UNPROFOR are reaching a point of decision over the use of NATO air in support of the mission." [Interpretation] And we will see further on: [In English] "... destruction of SAM sites and EW facilities" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We all can read, Mr. Karadzic. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is this, General, sir: Do you see that amongst your ranks, there was full awareness that you were being disinformed, that fire was opened on us, and when we responded, NATO air-strikes were being called for and prepared?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that that letter was an accurate reflection of what we thought at the time, but I don't think it accurately reflects what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it says here that UNPROFOR will be at war if attacks are launched and destruction from -- and so on and so forth: [In English] "UNPROFOR would be at war. This position has been discussed and they are as one about it." [Interpretation] A full agreement that if you open fire, you will be at war with us, right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we're referring to is going for higher-level targets, which is, as I've explained in the past to you, we were not prepared to do because it was not compatible with the peacekeeping mission that we had been given by the Security Council. NATO was keen on widening the number of targets, the level of targets; we refused to do so, in spite of the fact that the Bosnian Serb side by then were firing SAM 2 intermediate and high-level missiles at the NATO aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One such installation was damaged by NATO and heavy artillery fire was opened on Mount Grmec, Petrovac and Kljuc. Although we had managed to reduce casualty through resourcefulness and other means. General, how did you call for those attacks? Who was it who you communicated with in NATO?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedures by which air-strikes were called from NATO was quite complex, but in simplified terms it consisted of me requesting the air-strikes, they had to be agreed I think in Zagreb, NATO would then respond. And the actual targeting of the NATO aircraft was done by UN soldiers on the ground. There was one category of use of force by NATO which did not involve the UN, and that is if the united -- if NATO aircraft felt that they were under any threat from our intermediate and high-level missiles as a result of being acquired by Serb radars, they had the right to fire at those radars and anti-aircraft sites without reference to the UN. The use of force at that point of course being one of self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about any other forms?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the only categories for the use of NATO in support of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that happened without your agreement and without you calling for them, but those that you called for, could you describe the route which you had to take from the moment you called for air-strikes to the moment air-strikes were approved. Who was you -- that you had to talk to? How did that transpire?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just explained it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder, Mr. Karadzic, how these lines of questions are relevant to your case, your indictment. Bear that in mind, and we have only limited time and I would like you to prioritise your questions. Move on to your next topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted and let me explain why this is important. This is important because we are going to ask documents from NATO, all the documents that pertain to us and attacks against us, because we have to shed light on the circumstances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have time -- you will have time to make your submission, but not now. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D712.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, if I'd known that you would not know enough about the beginning of attacks from Bihac and how much territory they had previously taken from us, I would bring you American maps which show you the situation day-in/day-out. However, do you accept that our counter-attack was preceded by a large-scale attack from Bihac against the Serbian Krajina, the Krajina of Bosnian Serbs, as described in this correspondence?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen the correspondence you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My letter to de Lapresle and Milovanovic's letters to you, and so on and so forth. The entire correspondence in which we are warning you that we were being attacked and that we would launch a counter-offensive. I just showed you all those a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said once before, I have no recall as to what the sequence of events were in the period leading up to the Bosnian Serb attack on Bihac. It could be as you said, that you were responding to a counter-attack; equally, it could be that you just attacked into the enclave for other reasons. We did not have military observers in a position to give us a blow-by-blow account of every single conflict that was happening in Bosnia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's go back to the total exclusion zone in the Sarajevo sector. Do you remember, General, that we had requested a proper definition of heavy artillery and that it was concluded that everything beyond a certain number of millimetres, which was 12.7 millimetres, fell under heavy artillery and should be withdrawn from the 20-kilometre zone?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sounds about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce 65 ter 1252 if it's not already in evidence as a Prosecution exhibit. Yes, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I please ask you to cast a glance at the document and especially at paragraph 3. Everybody can see everything, but paragraph 3 is particularly important: [In English] "We then met at the Presidency with Izetbegovic and Salajdzic, who said that they were willing to sign a cease-fire on condition that the Serb artillery moved out of range of Sarajevo and was also placed under the control of UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] Right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that we disputed over the term or the difference between term "monitoring" and "control"? We thought that monitoring was acceptable, whereas the Muslim side demanded that only the Serb weaponry be controlled. Am I right? Was that how things transpired?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember a general discussion on the distinction between monitoring and control, but that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember what it says here in paragraph 3 and that was that the Muslim side requested that only Serb weapons be controlled and they didn't offer for their weapons to be controlled in turn?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was their position, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the elements. It is a list of elements: "Effective control by UNPROFOR of certain key positions in and around Sarajevo. "On-site monitoring by UNPROFOR of all artillery, heavy mortars, and everything above 12.7 millimetres ... [In English] "The non-use of Sarajevo as a base from which to launch any attacks. "The freezing of the strength and movements of existing forces in and around Sarajevo." [Interpretation] Was that a fair concept, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it looks as though this was a draft of a document which I think I possibly have seen in the past, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the Serb side agreed to that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You certainly agreed to put your weapons under some form of UN control and to withdraw the rest from outside the 20-kilometre circle, yes, that is so. Of course the fact that you failed to comply in every case with that obligation didn't surprise us either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. You just tell us now whether the Muslim side agreed to that draft of yours?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember what the agreement with the Bosnian government side was without having reminder from a document or doing further research, but the general position was that they certainly agreed to stop use of their heavy weapons and stop troop movements and stop attacking from within Sarajevo. That was the general position which I think they agreed. They certainly didn't put their weapons under UN control in the way that the Bosnian Serb weapons were put under control. I think there was some symbolic gesture in one of the barracks where some weapons were produced, but certainly by no means did that constitute the handing-in of their weapons to the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D713.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the Court please produce 1D02458.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does the name Major Annink ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not a name I've seen or heard of for 14 years, but I think it probably does ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the first page of this document? Which is missing? It starts with page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It starts with paragraph 3, but that's the way we received it from the OTP. It must be part of a larger UN document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would now like to draw your attention to this paragraph further down: [In English] "To a question on the whereabouts of the Bosnian soldiers who were moving from Dobrinja towards Ilidza this morning Major Annink said they were with the troops and they entered the tunnel and possibly came out. "He further said that the 60-millimetre mortars, which the BiH soldiers were carrying, could be easily strapped on the back and it was very easy to carry those weapons." [Interpretation] Further on he explains that he believes this was not a violation of the total exclusion zone and that it's only mortars over 80 millimetres -- or rather, that everything beyond 12.7 millimetres is forbidden. Actually, do you remember that Muslim soldiers violated the agreement in this way as well?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the Bosnian state side forces did not comply with the agreement to cease firing from Sarajevo outwards immediately. And of course there were violations that occurred throughout the summer, but the general position was that one of reasonable calm which enabled us to start restoring utilities and run convoys in and out. There were violations on both sides, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will see who was the first to violate the agreement because I guess that matters, but we'll deal with that later. I'm just saying that Major Annink is giving a very creative interpretation of the agreement and that 80 millimetres does not seem to be more than 12.7 millimetres from his point of view. Basically he is justifying this carrying of 60-millimetre mortars strapped to soldiers' backs and -- well, it is an infantry weapon, but still it can be used for shooting, but don't you agree that this is a very creative interpretation and an incorrect one at that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, General. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was wondering when we were going to get to the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have in front of me the details as to what calibres of different weapons systems were part of the agreement to withdraw heavy weapons, and of course an 81-millimetre mortar probably was, a 60-millimetre mortar may not have been. I don't have any memory recall of that. I do remember that 12.7 cannons were the limit. And Major Annink, if I remember, was a press relations officer who was fielding questions from the press and this is a summary of the press conference which he had in Sarajevo. And I suspect that his position about the difference between a 60-millimetre mortar and an 81-millimetre mortar probably did reflect the agreement that had been made. I can't say one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]: [In English] "A journalist expressed his wonder that how was a 12.7-millimetre anti-aircraft gun regarded as a violation and not a 60-millimetre mortar." [Interpretation] That's the point, just that. General, you do accept that Muslim weapons were being viewed differently; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I guess the agreement was sort of supposed to apply both ways, and as I say, I can't remember what the discussion on the millimetrage of the weapons had to be withdrawn was. So I can't make any further contribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has this been admitted? Does it have a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D714, Your Honours.
