utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It has a first page actually, Your Honours, which my colleague Mr. Reid has been able to locate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That could be added to this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm also advised that this must be a seven-page document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We've only been able to come up with five so far, so that's one more than previously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit this as it is, and then if the -- we'll add those two pages and see what we can do else other than that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence is very interested in what those two pages say. Perhaps it's something related to Rule 68. 1D2450, could we have that document now, please. 1D2450. I believe we don't have the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you recognise this? This is a press release. It's press releases and summaries of UNPROFOR, right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 15th of February, 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the date on the top.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we then have page 3 from here I mean, three pages further on. It's the second page of the document. Could you zoom in a bit, the top part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, General, can you see this? There is this meeting, Mr. Akashi, General Rose met with Admiral Boorda, Commander-in-Chief of Allied Forces Southern Europe at Pleso airport. "The purpose of the meeting was to promote closer co-ordination between UNPROFOR and NATO in relation to the possible use of air power in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in particular in the Sarajevo area." Both Mr. Akashi and Admiral Boorda emphasised that if NATO used air power at the request of the UN, it would be done in an impartial manner, in an impartial way, and would be directed at any party violating the cease-fire. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many times did the Muslim side violate the cease-fire? According to your very own texts, many more times than the Serb side; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the summer of 1994, I think that probably would be an accurate assessment. But again, I don't have the figures in front of me. What I do know is that the major breakdown of that agreement which occurred in September of 1994 was the result of the actions of the Bosnian government side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what you said: [In English] "General Rose told journalists that many of the cease-fire violations that had taken place on Saturday night had been committed by the Bosnian Presidency Forces and not by the Bosnian Serb army." [Interpretation] How many times were the Muslim forces bombed by NATO?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, to reply to your question I would have to put the question into context. When Admiral Boorda and Mr. Akashi met at Pleso airport and had this discussion, NATO position, as you can see, is that they would respond to violations on either side as a result of requests from United Nations. In fact, we didn't expect the cease-fire to be immediate, a hundred per cent successful, and we expected some untidy results between the signing of the cease-fire and the stopping of the firing around Sarajevo; and that's exactly what happened. By the end of that summer General Boorda -- Admiral Boorda had been replaced by Admiral Smith. It was clear that NATO had changed its position in terms of the use of force against all parties who violated, in particular their own ultimatum for the demilitarisation of Sarajevo. And from that moment on, NATO took sides and, regrettably, that finally dragged the United Nations protection forces on the ground into being seen as being partial by the Bosnian Serb side. That is what happened. So to discuss who was firing at who in February and why NATO didn't respond would require a different reply from me to what happened in the end of the summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly when you say here in the transcript partial by the Bosnian -- [In English] Had they been in favour of Bosnian Serb side or against Bosnian Serb side? Maybe my English knowledge is not --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll just read what is written. Yes, the Bosnian Serb side started to see the UN as being partial. It ceased to regard them as being impartial; i.e., you started to believe that we were now siding with the Bosnian government side as a result of the failure by NATO to act impartially. Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D715.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D02451. 1D02451.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I remind you that this is a telegram dated the 20th of February, 1994, 1756 to Annan, Stoltenberg, Rose, from Mr. Akashi - so to all three sides. Mr. Akashi is describing a meeting with Karadzic and with Izetbegovic. So please focus on the paragraph entitled: Meeting with Karadzic in Pale on the 19th of February: [In English] "Regarding the definition of UNPROFOR 'control' of re-grouped weapons, Dr. Karadzic raised no objection to our definition, although he emphasised their right to self-defence, therefore the right of regaining their weapons in the event of attacks from the Muslim side." [Interpretation] Do you remember that Mr. Akashi informed you about this by way of this letter?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3: [In English] "Dr. Karadzic also reiterated that UNPROFOR elements should be deployed on all sites, and should have complete freedom of movement in the entire zone, as agreed to previously." [Interpretation] You remember this as well, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now 3: [In English] "Dr. Karadzic also expressed his eagerness to open direct routes into and around Sarajevo" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, paragraph 3 we should remain on the previous page in the middle.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's right. It's the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we can see what it is that I had proposed. I had proposed that joint check-points be established, that is to say UNPROFOR and the Bosnian Serb army and on the other side the Bosnian army and UNPROFOR. Do you remember that too?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now let us see what was recorded from the meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 6 -- or rather 7: [In English] "Despite all our efforts, I have observed the continuing tendency by the Bosnian side to feed and encourage the 'incident hungry' press in Sarajevo." [Interpretation] So even from Ambassador Akashi's level it was noted that the Muslim side is creating events, as it were, in order to feed the media in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can see it was written there and I agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D716.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you also agreed -- or rather, it went without saying that if we were attacked we had the right to get our weapons back from those collection points; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we ever agreed that, no. And in fact, when you did come and seize some weapons from one of the collecting points, in particular a T-55 tank, we called on NATO air-strikes in order to get that tank returned, which it duly was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D2481.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, General, that Muslims fired from outside the 20-kilometre zone at Serbs within the 20-kilometre zone? They were firing from the centre of town itself and also from Central Bosnia, like Visoko and so on.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it was written there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a telegram sent by Ambassador Akashi to Secretary Annan, Gharekhan, Stoltenberg, and this is what paragraph 2 says -- have all the participants read this, actually? Can we move on to the second page. Then we're going to have a look at the map to see how things stand there. Can we move on to the second page. Now let us look at 3: [In English] "The Protocol to the Sarajevo WCP Agreement on 14th of February ... (attached) recognises the BSA's legitimate right to self-defence. If the BSA comes under more pressure from the BiH, their demand to have access to their weapons could become a more pressing reality, under the Protocol referred to above." [Interpretation] You see that there was a protocol after all and that it codified our right to take our weapons if we were attacked; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we now have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, is that the way it was, General? Is it not clearly stated here that the United Nations were aware of the fact that we had this right to self-defence too?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, reading that paragraph I -- it doesn't alter my view that the -- at the time the UN position certainly in Sarajevo was that we had weapons collected up in weapon collecting points to prevent any further firing on Sarajevo, and that if those weapons were withdrawn from those sides we would respond accordingly. This discussion between Mr. Akashi and his senior advisors and bosses in New York is something I was not privy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, now we are discussing exceptions, or rather, situations in which we were allowed to take our weapons back and defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move two pages on to see the protocol that was signed. One more page. Those are signatures, my own and Mr. Akashi's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this is the content of the protocol. I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 1, please: [In English] "In the event that UNPROFOR withdraws for any reason from mutually-agreed sides of the re-grouping of heavy weapons without the agreement of the BSA or that it withdraws from its interposition areas between the Serb and Muslim lines, the BSA reserves the right to re-deploy its weapons and increase troop levels on the front lines, while in event of a Muslim attack on the Serbs which UNPROFOR is not able either prevent or stop immediately, the BSA reserves the right to implement adequate measures of self-determination -- self-defence." Self-determination will come yet.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that is a statement of the Bosnian Serb position as reflected by Mr. Akashi in this summary of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a position. This is the protocol. This is the most important point in the protocol that was signed by Mr. Akashi and myself. This is not my own one-sided statement. This is something that the United Nations and I agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it says quite clearly in paragraph 1: "In the event that UNPROFOR withdraws ...," of course we had no intention of withdrawing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it also says if a Muslim attack takes place, one that you will not or cannot prevent, that we have the right to organise our own self-defence; isn't that right? That's the second part of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, as I say, it's a hypothetical situation that's being agreed here because the United Nations had no intention of withdrawing from either Sarajevo or the weapon collecting points. Obviously if we abandon those weapons then you would have the right to get them back, presumably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to another possibility here, namely that you had not left; rather, we had been attacked by the Muslims. So would you agree that this is a basis, a legal basis, for our right to take back the weapons that we had handed over to you for your supervision? It's not your withdrawal that we're talking about here. We're talking about this other option, if the Muslims attack. Was this not something that both Akashi and I had signed up to?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the document, it looks as if the - and this is my interpretation now - is that if the pressures on the Bosnian Serb side required you to reinforce your positions outside Sarajevo somewhere else, then possibly you might have been allowed to take the weapons that were in the weapon collecting point and redeploy them elsewhere in Bosnia. But I can't say that that is exactly how I understood it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that all the participants can see, General, that this only refers to the total exclusion zone in Sarajevo. If we are attacked in Sarajevo, we can defend ourselves in Sarajevo. Why would we defend ourselves in Bijeljina if we were attacked in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D717, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 13636.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with this map and this circle?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, apart from the fact that it's not one of a UN maps and that I think you may have shown it to me the other day, it reflects the original UN map with which I am familiar, showing the original position of the epicentre of the 20-kilometre circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that's the centre by the church at Marin Dvor; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's, I think, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, General, that you protested - and we saw a document just a while ago - and you said that beyond that circle the Muslim forces had not been demilitarised, or in other words that they did not have an exclusion zone and that they fired at Ilijas in the very north of the map and that they also opened fire on the Serbs within the zone?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly remember firing at Ilijas, yes. Where the fire came from, I don't know, either from within or from without the 20-kilometre circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you to be assisted by the usher --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, do we not have a picture of this of better quality? This seems to be a scanned one of map 25 of the Sarajevo binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll check, Your Honour, but I'm inclined to think of this one probably not. We have pictures of other maps depicting the same area of better quality and enlarged, but not of this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you're happy to go on with this picture, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if it were better, it would be better. But what is important is this total exclusion zone, a 20-kilometre-wide circle. If this map has been admitted, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I note it is map 25 or page 25 of the Sarajevo-specific court binder. We will admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D718, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the Court please produce 65 ter 6863, 65 ter 6863.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With your permission, I would like to simplify things. This is General de Lapresle's telegram sent to Secretary Annan and Stoltenberg in Geneva about heavy weapons exclusion zone violation, where it says under 1: "The daily situation report says that there was the heaviest fighting since February ..." And it goes on to say: [In English] "... approximately 300 mortar rounds and 6.000 small arms. The attack was initiated by BH Army and was supported by mortars firing from residential areas within the city limits centred ..." [Interpretation] And then: [In English] "The BH assaulted the Sharpstone feature ..." [Interpretation] This Sharpstone feature is something that we will deal with with other witnesses. [In English] "The BiH also launched a feint in the Jewish cemetery. Unconfirmed reports from the BSA liaison officer said the BSA lost ground in the Sharpstone area and suffered two dead and five wounded. These initial attacks were followed by a restrained BSA response using heavy weapons." [Interpretation] Do you agree, General, that this was something that fell through as a Muslim attack unfolded against Serb positions? This is something that you mentioned yourself in September?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the day very well indeed, and I think initially the Serb responses were moderate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that at first there was a lot of restraint.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page and see what you're talking about. You're talking about the Serb responses. [In English] "The BSA responded, targeting the Zetra stadium ... the Presidency, the area north of the cathedral and Sedrenik. The commander -- BH command called on both sides to immediately cease all military actions or he would be obliged to take all appropriate measures to protect the civilian population of Sarajevo, including air-strikes." [Interpretation] Do you remember that you resorted to those arguments?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the second sentence in paragraph 2 where it says that the BiH side initiated the attack and that the VRS response was both defensive and restrained and that in that situation we did not withdraw our weapons from the collection points. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me to agree with something I wrote. Of course it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the assessment part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "This may have been in retaliation for the Serbs cutting off utilities in Sarajevo. It is also apparent with President Izetbegovic visiting New York on the 18th that it was an attempt by the BH to elicit a strong response from the BSA. The BiH may have hoped that the BSA would withdraw heavy weapons from the weapon collection points and that NATO would respond with air-strikes." [Interpretation] Further on: [In English] "With Haiti dominating US and international news, the BiH wished to both move Sarajevo back onto the front page as well as once again paint the Bosnian Serb army as aggressors ..." and so on and so on. [Interpretation] Do you see the hardships we suffered? We didn't have a choice. We were not allowed to defend because there were the media, there was NATO, everybody was waiting for us. You yourself said that we were under a lot of pressure by NATO and the media; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly can't reply to your comment because of course it's a description of your own motivations and position at the time. All I could do was report what I saw certainly around me on the ground, and it's -- my thoughts in this letter are ones which I still hold today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see that you noticed, or, rather, you believed that the Muslims were moving around with mortars, they fired at Serbs, and that you had an impression that the VRS was using more weapons than they did. And under (b): "Making it more difficult for the Army of Republika Srpska or indeed NATO to pin-point the weapons and to retaliate against them." And (c): "By confusing the areas the shelling came from, encourage indiscriminate and multi-targeting by the BSA [In English] With resultant civilian casualties." [Interpretation] This is a very clever perception on your part, General, and I would like to thank you of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is this: Was that a clever perception? And the next question: Why were we bombed on the 22nd of September, three days thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember why the NATO air-strikes were called in September, but I guess it was because you had moved some heavy weapons out of the weapon collecting point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document's already an exhibit and it's been re-read almost in totality into the record all over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was about to point out that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That was Exhibit P1673.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The following one has not been admitted, it's 65 ter 19266, 19266 from UNMO Pale, a letter that was forwarded by them and originally drafted by General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was sent to the UNPROFOR command and look at the first paragraph. It says here that: "On the 22nd of September ... between 1840 and 1910 hours NATO aircraft launched a brutal attack against" us "in the region of the village of Dobrosevici" inhabited mostly by civilian population. You can all read that this happened after Muslim forces organised armed attacks over several days from the part of city of Sarajevo under Muslim forces control against the 20-kilometre zone around Sarajevo. You can see the entire text, General. And at the bottom it says: [In English] "Having estimated the situation which has arisen, particularly bombing the Serb civilian population, the UNPROFOR command's giving help and support to the Muslim side, we inform you that, until further notice, we are unable to approve and insure the UN peace forces activities on the territory of the Republic of Srpska." [Interpretation] General, whatever actions were undertaken by the VRS in their relations with UNPROFOR, there were good reasons. In September on 22nd of September, there was a prevalent opinion that we didn't have weapons, that we were restrained in our responses and actions, and still we were bombarded on the 22nd of September. An order came from the United Nations and a person is in the field from the United Nations, a gunner was already there.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In war things are very fast-moving, Dr. Karadzic, and what may have been the case on the 22nd of September when I wrote that analysis, the situation changed dramatically after you took a tank from a weapon collecting point and also opened fire, if I remember right, on a French vehicle with that tank. At that point the dynamic changed and air-strikes were inevitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here we don't see any information about that. That may have been an incident that involved the French later on. But, General, prior to that all the time the Muslims violated the provisions of the total exclusion zone. They launched fierce attacks against us. Nobody reacted. And then when we seize a piece of weaponry, we were bombed. Pursuant to the protocol, we had the right to defend ourselves. That right was something that the United Nations signed up to; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the topic of our trial is not why NATO bombed. Use your time efficiently.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not putting NATO on trial. That's not my intention. What I'm trying to prove is that our relationship with UNPROFOR is not an ill-will without any motives, but rather that there were good reasons for our suspicions, for our cautions, and -- towards the United Nations because those same United Nations commanded bombardment in our territory and they even had gunners on the ground. But let's leave it at that. Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D719.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D02463 is the next document I would like to call up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a telegram sent by Mr. Akashi to Gharekhan, Stoltenberg, relative to General Delic's visit to New York. If you look at the third paragraph and you will see that during the visit General Delic stated that UNPROFOR had disarmed Muslim Bosnian forces in the safe areas and therefore has a moral obligation to protect them, which was not correct, as you know, right? You did not disarm anybody, did you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we've already discussed that when the agreement was made regarding Srebrenica and Zepa, the United Nations Security Council Resolutions hadn't yet come into effect and that a local agreement was made between the two sides to disarm the -- for the one side to withdraw, for the other side to disarm. And of course the Bosnian government side in Srebrenica chose to only hand in useless weapons and kept control of their own useful weapons and returned over the next few months to their policy of attacking from within the enclave the Serbs who surrounded them. That is true. But of course the passing or the accepting of United Nations Security Council Resolutions did not, as we've discussed, call on the Bosnian government forces in the enclaves to disarm. So there were two slightly different situations prevailing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here Mr. Akashi disputes General Delic's positions and he says: [In English] "In view of estimated strength of BH forces in pockets," and so on and so on, "we believe that neither Srebrenica nor Zepa are fully demilitarised." [Interpretation] And that's very much in keeping what we have just heard from you. Can we go to the following page. The last paragraph says that: "Finally Bosnia-Herzegovina commander reported that relations with the Bosnian side on the whole remained good. [In English] There are, however, significant restrictions on UNPROFOR freedom of movement along the confrontation line from Visoko to Breza and east of Tuzla. In addition, a CanBat 2 observation post was directly targeted by the BiH on 15th of September and 16th of September, despite strong protests to the Presidency as well as to General Delic." [Interpretation] Do you remember that the restrictions on your movements applied in the Muslim territory and that the Canadian observation post was fired at on the 15th and 16th September?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember those particular incidents, but I can repeat what I've already said, and that is that the United Nations protection force and the aid convoys came under repeated obstruction and from time to time attacked by all three warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D720.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it the time for our next break or shall I move on to the topic of the demilitarised zone on Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break now for 25 minutes. We'll resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before we continue, I wanted to confirm with you, Mr. Tieger, that the order of witnesses hasn't been changed in relation to the upcoming two witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Conclude your cross-examination by 6.30, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the Court please produce 1D02466.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Until then, General, let me ask you, do you know that my vice-presidents, Professor Plavsic and Professor Koljevic, were also vice-presidents of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Joint Presidency of the state?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've certainly met them both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you know that from 1990 to 1992 were members of the Joint Presidency? Not of Republika Srpska but of the entire state of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a statement, Dr. Karadzic, or a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A question. My question is this: Did you know that they were members of the Joint Presidency before they left it when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have known that at the time. I certainly have no memory of it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When I'm saying that we were equal parties, I'm corroborating this with the fact that they were members of the Joint Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Please pay attention to this telegram sent by His Excellency Mr. Akashi to Annan, Gharekhan, Goulding, and Stoltenberg. In the first paragraph the first sentence says this: [In English] "It has been apparent in the last few days that the Bosnian government is deliberately creating obstacles to the withdrawal of its troops from Mount Igman and the re-establishment of the integrity of the demilitarised zone." [Interpretation] Could you tell the Trial Chamber in the shortest possible terms what was the story of Igman or would you like me to give you statements or assertions and ask you what you think about them and state your opinion with regard to all of my assertions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Serbian army took Mount Igman and Mount Bjelasnica in August 1993?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that that was considered the full encirclement of Sarajevo and that we were given an ultimatum to withdraw?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that before that and after that the Muslim forces from Sarajevo and into Sarajevo -- or rather, that they could enter and leave Sarajevo either via Igman or through the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a route which lay down Mount Igman and then the second part of the route was under the airport through the tunnel or around the end of the airfield at the opposite end from Lukavica. But they had to come down Mount Igman if all other routes were blocked to get into Sarajevo. But of course the military convoys or military movements were not permitted by the UN. These were civilian convoys. I should make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that we did withdraw and that we handed over the zone on Mount Igman to the United Nations and then that zone was declared a demilitarised zone on Igman pursuant to an agreement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 4 in this document. Page 4, the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a copy of the agreement on the setting up of -- or rather, on the withdrawal of the forces from Mount Igman and Bjelasnica signed by Stjepan Siber on behalf of the Muslim army and Milovanovic on behalf of the Serb army and witnessed by Brigadier Vere Hayes?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, that is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go back to the first page. Is it correct that the United Nations managed to secure that area as a demilitarised zone, at least for a while?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ultimatum to demilitarise the zone came from NATO not from the UN, but it was supported by the UN on the ground, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that the VRS handed the zone over to the United Nations, to UNPROFOR, and not to either NATO or the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Muslims abused the agreement. They took the zone and passed by the undefended area and killed our medical personnel, 16 men and four women?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And after that did that lead to a Crisis Staff because they didn't want to abandon the demilitarised zone for a long time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb forces you're referring to or the Bosnian state forces, the Bosnian government forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The forces of the Bosnian Serbs withdrew and handed the demilitarised zone over to the United Nations, and after that the Muslim forces re-took that area and they didn't want to withdraw; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They intruded into that area. They didn't re-take the whole area. They moved -- they advanced into the area. They were stopped from any further advance by the UN, but they refused to withdraw. They were stationed at that point inside the military zone, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I draw your attention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say inside the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, demilitarised zone I should have said or probably swallowed my prefix.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We saw the first sentence and can we now look at the last sentence of the first paragraph: [In English] "The letter from Ambassador Sacirbey now appears to confirm the increasing suspicion that the government in fact is trying through all possible means to go back on its commitment to re-establish the integrity of the demilitarised zone." [Interpretation] In other words, they didn't want for the demilitarisation to take effect; right? And can you also look at the first two sentences in paragraph 2. Again they speak about the same agreement that we have already shown. Do you remember all that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what we can read in paragraph 3: " ... in May 1994 UNPROFOR HQ showed that the BiH side had infiltrated and started setting up positions on Mount Igman in violation of the agreement" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's all repetition of what the witness has already confirmed. I don't think you need to read out all those statements while complaining about --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- shortage of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we then see paragraph 6 which says that there were 1.000 shells fired. And then the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In a nutshell, General, do you remember that the United Nations had major problems in securing the withdrawal of the Muslim forces from the demilitarised zone on Mount Igman and that that was also why our relations intensified even further or were aggravated even further?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you see on that same page under 6, the end of paragraph 6, that outside of the exclusion zone BiH forces are firing on the Serbs within the exclusion zone [as interpreted]. We've already spoken about that. In other words, there were no exclusion zones in Visoko and Breza, they opened and fired on us from Central Bosnia. In other words, do you remember, General, that some elements of their forces remained even after you had left Bosnia? Is it true that for a long, long time -- or rather, that it took a long, long time for the status of a demilitarised zone to be reinstated?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when that happened or if indeed it happened because I left at the end of January 1994 -- 1995, and of course it was still an ongoing problem at the time I left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the transcript should read differently. The transcript says the BiH forces are firing on the Serbs within the exclusion zone, I think that should be the other way around. But, General, could you explain to me what the last sentence of that paragraph means. However, this is a situation which is not within either UNPROFOR or NATO's mandate to control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if I remember, sir, the Cemerska plateau where this fighting was taking place was to the south-west, I think, of Mount Igman and it was not an area which we had any observation of or control over. So what was happening there we couldn't give a clear view of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, General, Mount Cemersko is a bit to the north of Vogosca within the 20-kilometre exclusion zone and it is being fired at out from outside the zone, from Breza and Visoko. We can look at the map and show Mount Cemersko there. Do you remember that it's between Vogosca and Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well I stand corrected in that case. I always thought it was referring to some fighting which broke out in the autumn south-west of Sarajevo and Mount Igman, but clearly you're referring to the fighting by Ilijas and Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, paragraph 7 says that they were throwing mines into the total exclusion zone at Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page now, please. It has to do with your letter to Ganic. That's not it. Just a moment. It might be one page further. Yes, one page further, please. No. I'll try to find the ERN number now. I'm going to read it and we're going to put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, General, that on the 16th of October you wrote a letter to Ganic and a copy was sent to Izetbegovic. It says: [In English] "I want to record my deep concern that the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina has not yet withdrawn its troops from the position of Mount Igman, especially in the area the west of Krupac in accordance with the 14th of August agreement." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. I'm going to hand the letter over to you now: [In English] "My troops are placed on Mount Igman at the request of your government. If you are unable to sustain the agreement with regard to your own troops' disposition, I will have to reconsider whether the forces under my command should remain on Mount Igman ..." and so on.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember writing a letter like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. If this letter is not part of this document under this number in e-court, then I'm going to ask -- I mean if it's not part of any Prosecution exhibit, could I tender it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I can't answer immediately as to whether it's part of any Prosecution exhibit, but I certainly have no objection to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll give it a number and sort it out later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't seen a copy of the document, so I can't ascertain whether it's genuine or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, take a look, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... a description --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is definitely my letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D721, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D02468. Actually, the previous document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, and you are minded to tender the previous document, Mr. Akashi's letter, 1D2466? That will be admitted as Exhibit D722.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are quite a few documents there and I thought that this letter of General Rose's was included as well; however, we have tendered it now. This is a rather complex document. There are quite a few documents related to the same thing. You can see in e-court how many pages there are. It's an original United Nations document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I just wanted to be fair to the Prosecutors. It's not just the first page. There are several documents. All of them are originals -- I mean under the same number, they're being tendered under the same number. 1D02468, can we have that now, please. Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this memorandum dated the 29th of October that pertains to the Bosnian Muslim violation of the demilitarised zone? This is a summary.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing this before, but I probably did see it. If I saw more of it, I might be able to have a better recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the first page it says -- on the first page it says: [In English] "General Rose will send a letter to the President on the 30th of October detailing the events in this summary and expressing his displeasure with the BiH action. The use of close air support will be mentioned in both the communication and the letter from General Rose. Appropriate measures will be taken by the Sector during this event."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see page 9 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's a press release. Let us see why there was a reference to close air support. Let us see whether conditions had been created. Please have a look at this: [In English] "Despite the agreements concluded on August 1993 regarding the DMZ on Mount Igman and assurances given by President Izetbegovic to order troops to evacuate that area, B&H forces have commenced this morning at 6.30 an offensive against Bosnian Serbs. Starting from DMZ, south of Javorak, the Bosnians used heavy weapons" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Karadzic, we can read it, as can General. Can you put your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please then have a look at this document, General. Had conditions been created to call NATO in, in order to discipline the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly had, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did NATO attack? Did NATO attack them and stop them?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained that by then NATO had -- policies had changed and they were not prepared to use any force at all against the Bosnian government forces, even though they were in direct violation of what was in fact a NATO ultimatum, not a UN ultimatum. That is the case as it -- as it unfolded at that time. And I was certainly advised by NATO that only a request or any request to use air-strikes against the Bosnian government forces would be denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D723, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So much for equality, equality of rights, equality of the two sides.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2478, can we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No comment, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw the comment. 1D2478, can we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this UNMO Pale sending a letter to the command in Pale, attention General Rose? It's a protest of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, the 7th of December, 1994; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can see that signal was sent by you to Mr. Akashi, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Headquarters in Sarajevo and to you too. Can you see, General, that the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska is providing information, or rather, lodging a protest primarily because of the attack or attacks launched by the Republic of Croatia in the western part of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the signal you sent, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see that it concerns hospitals, schools, places of worship, residential areas, that all of them had been bombed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, did you know about this? Did NATO and the UN do something about stopping the regular forces of Croatia in this campaign against the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly can't remember discussing this incident with Mr. Akashi and what action he took. I don't know. We didn't have troops deployed in that area, so any information would have come from one of the two sides in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd submit this is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Agreed. What is your question in relation to this document, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my question is whether it was only the Muslims who were under protection or did this pertain to Croats too? Could anybody attack and hunt down the Serbs unpunished? Is this information to the effect that we're being attacked by Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have 15 minutes; otherwise, I take it you've exhausted all your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this document being admitted? The letter was received by the General and it shows the situation that we were in, Excellency, that's my point, the situation we were in. When we are defending ourselves, we get bombed; and when everybody attacks us, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No comment, Mr. Karadzic. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D724, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I now please have in e-court - we haven't got much time for documents anymore - could we have General Rose's book in e-court. It is number 1D1037. However, it's probably under a different number of the OTP as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that book, pages of the book are admitted under Exhibit D162.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, may I remind you, the late Eve-Anne Prentice in the case against President Milosevic, she testified and said that Sarajevo was a divided city, not a city under siege because the line went through single apartment buildings as well. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who this person is and what they said, but I'll agree that the line of conflict went through buildings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have page 53 and 54, the bottom of 53 and the top of 54, in which you say in a spirited way how the journalists had confused Sarajevo and Baghdad. It's got to be somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it Mr. Arnett's report when he was working for CNN, I think you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 53 in hard copy you mean, Mr. Karadzic? Page 53?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it should be 53.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bottom of 53, last line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yeah, since there is no such thing as a tidy end --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it's from there up until "leave Bosnia" on the other page. So I would like to tender those two pages. And then 54 and 55 where you say what Muhamed Sacirbey said at the UN about what was going on in Sarajevo. He's saying all of that from sunny Miami, whereas from your own window you can see that things are actually different, right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So 53, 54, and 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We now have page 161. In the book itself, 161. General, I would like to draw your attention to the following paragraph: [In English] On the 10th of August, a Bosnian army T-55 tank" -- [Interpretation] It should be 161.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Serbian tanks. So you saw for yourself that a tank was leaving the tunnel and firing and then a 120-millimetre mortar fired at the Serbs from the Kosevo Hospital compound and you asked for support --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we dealt with it. Did you say "Serbian tanks," Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, August 10th. It refers to a Muslim tank that was leaving the tunnel and firing and there's this mortar that was firing at the Serbs from the Kosevo Hospital compound. Thank you. So page 161. Now 163, two ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your observation is: In mid-August the Bosnians were bombing Ilijas that was on the outskirts and within the zone -- so we would like to tender this page as well. Could we now have the following pages -- or actually, can we deal with your assistance with pages 170 through 174. It is about the letter written by Admiral Smith to General de Lapresle. Pages 170 through 174. It starts with "on the 11th of September ..." Have we found it? So it's 170 through 174. It must be down towards the bottom. Do you agree that this is your description of the situation, or rather, of an attempt made by NATO to take-over the powers of the United Nations in order to be able to act more freely; right? Page 170. [In English] "At the meeting I dismissed the idea that UNPROFOR had gone soft on the Serbs or was allowing a reimposition of the Siege of Sarajevo as nonsense. The Serbs had not halted the delivery of aid into Sarajevo, although the recent offensives by the Bosnian army had caused the Serbs to deny the passage of commercial traffic into the city."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm at a loss to know what question I'm answering here. Obviously this -- if you're reading accurately from my book, that's what I wrote at the time and that's what I still believe. NATO had ceased to be impartial by then, by the autumn of 1994. We've discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to tender these three or four pages or five from 170 through 174.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is a part of your book that will assist us in shedding light on the situation as it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move on to page 180. 180: [In English] "The 22nd of September, Karadzic had told Sergio de Mello that the partiality of the UN was no longer tolerable. He agreed that the demilitarisation of Sarajevo was an attractive idea that should be persuade, although this was dependant upon the Muslims agreeing on total cessation of hostilities in Bosnian." [Interpretation] Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 188: [In English] "I had wondered many times about the extent of Izetbegovic's complicity in the profiteering that arose through his army's control of the tunnel ...," and so on. [Interpretation] Until this part: [In English] "... I believe he knew exactly what was going on in Bosnia, and was personally responsible for the decision to keep his forces inside the demilitarised zone on Mount Igman." [Interpretation] That was also your position, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 191 and 192.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 191 and 192: [In English] "On my return, there was a foreign office telegram waiting for me telling me that Muhamed Sacirbey, the Bosnian representative ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "... in the UN in New York, had delivered a protest against my demand that Bosnian army should withdraw ...," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] And now let us look at all of it. Let's just go through it: [In English] "The Bosnians hurled grenades down the slope at the French and fired rockets at their vehicle fortunately without causing serious injury. By dawn, Gobillard had driven the Bosnians out of the demilitarised zone with the exception of one small isolated person ..." [Interpretation] All the way up to here: [In English] "The next day, Major Indjic ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "... when I told this to Gus [phoen] for the first time during my tour, he looked slightly thoughtful." [Interpretation] So they were firing when General Gobillard was moving them from the demilitarised zone, they were firing at the French, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I take it that your position is that you will be tendering this book in pieces? Just parts -- only those parts you referred to will be tendered?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only today but also yesterday and the day before yesterday. But I know that the book has been tendered, but only the pages thereof have been tendered and not the entire book. The entire book would be too much for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, do you take any position as to the book?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I actually have no objection to the book coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will be benefitted in terms of full understanding if we have it in its entirety. So you don't have to refer to it in every part, but you can make submission later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see another document, the last document, which has been admitted already. I would just like to remind the General of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you agree that a cease-fire is very much dependent on both sides; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, so we admit the book in its entirety. The number was already given, Exhibit D162. Yes, you -- is that your last question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. 65 ter 6667 is the next document I would like to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My thesis, General, is this: When both sides honoured a cease-fire, the cease-fire held. When the Muslims were interested in a cease-fire, that cease-fire held. I would like to remind you of a situation when that football game was played. I supported that because Sarajevo was my club as well. I would like to read the sentence starting with "Moreover": "Moreover, the further normalisation of life in Sarajevo is in our interest ..." General, did you believe and did you see in many documents that our interest was the normalisation of life in Sarajevo, not only because of the 70.000 Serbs, but also because of the Muslims? If you don't believe that, then you have to believe that we suffered from a lot of pressures. Sarajevo all of a sudden was in the spotlight on the front pages of all the media?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that your strategic interests in 1994 was to halt the fighting, have a cease-fire, and in your terms trade the land which you agreed to give up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and thank you for coming here to testify. Thank you for having met with the Defence and I would like to thank you for your patience during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you begin, Ms. Edgerton, the Chamber has some questions for the witness. Judge Baird. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: General, in the proceedings of the 6th of October - and this is at page 7333 of the LiveNote transcript - you stated that what happened on Mount Igman was that the Bosnian government forces started to launch attacks across Mount Igman to the demilitarised zone at the Serb positions on the other side, and NATO who was responsible for enforcing the demilitarisation of that area had failed to take action against the government forces. And this is in spite of the fact that you protested to the Bosnian government that they should desist in doing this. They continued to do so. And when you asked NATO to take action, they refused. Now, would you say, General, that NATO's refusal to take action would have emboldened the Bosnian government to continue in that way?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly would have done so and indeed it did so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: It did so. Thank you. Now, just page 763 [sic] of the LiveNote transcript, General. Dr. Karadzic referred you to a UN report of the 7th of February, 1994, where it was stated: "The media reported General Rose's statement that it was not known who fired as the shell had first hit some stalls and changed its trajectory." And he had asked you whether you had known more than you do now. Now, your answer was, amongst other things, that if it was your major statement to the press about the market-place bombing, then it was an incomplete report of your statement because you went on to state that it was not possible to say specifically who had fired the bomb, but in your opinion it was most likely to have been fired by the Serbs because of the events two days before. Now, can you tell us, General, whether at any time you had said that the shell had first hit some stalls and changed its trajectory, any time at all?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have done so, but I can't remember making that statement. Certainly I was briefed to that effect by the initial inspection team that went to the site. But I may have referred to that in a press statement or even in a written statement somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: One last question, General, and I shan't detain you further. At page 7367, in respect of that very bombing, Dr. Karadzic stated that from the first moment onwards, the Serb side was clearly stating that they requested an investigation. They wanted proper insight and they wanted to participate in the investigation. He then asked: "Was the Serb side allowed to do that?" And you answered that: "The team that was formed did not include the Serb side," and you had no memory or recall as to why that was the case. The second team was put together in Zagreb by Mr. Akashi. Why it was decided that there should not be a representative from the Bosnian Serb side you had no idea. Now, General, would you say then that from the outset that investigative team, as it was constituted, lacked balance?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was balanced in that it had neither Bosnian government side nor Bosnian Serb side representation on it, if my memory is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I see, so neither side was represented?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my memory of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I begin, just two small administrative things. We've replaced the map, 65 ter number 13636 with a better version and it's been uploaded in e-court. And yesterday at T7442, there was discussion about the translation of D690, and CLSS translation of that document for this exhibit's now been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me, Mr. President, just on one other administrative note, I just wanted to indicate that there were a number of documents that we didn't get to with the examination of General Rose that we'll be moving to admit through the bar table. I just wanted to make that clear now so no one's surprised when that comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, to go back through the evidence that you've given over the course of the last few days, I'd like to touch on something you mentioned with regard to sniping and it was at page 7293, line 25, to 7294, line 4, of the transcript. There you were asked a question by Dr. Karadzic about the interview you had had at the jail, and the question read: "You confirmed that the United Nations could not determine unequivocally and with precision from where sniper fire had come because there weren't any proper investigations that would have established that beyond a reasonable doubt." And your answer was: "That's so." Now, what I'd like to know, General, is whether you see any contradiction between this evidence that you'd given and that which we find in paragraph 217 of your written evidence, your statement, which talks about the overall responsibility for the greater proportion of the sniping incidents on the civilian population of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sector Sarajevo were the organ which was the French Brigade deployed in Sarajevo was the body responsible for reporting sniping incidents as well as the United Nations military observers. But the coverage was very sparse. The best way of knowing what the level of sniping was came from the casualties lists, and that was the basis on which I said the majority of the sniping had been from the Serb side to the Bosnian government side across the line. And that was the impression which I think was universally held. Now, of course the argument could have been produced that we didn't know what the casualty lists on the other side were, although we did have UNMOs there. But I think the general view was the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to move on to go back to the subject of Gorazde and a question you were asked at the outset of today. Dr. Karadzic told you today that in your book on page 161 you confirmed that the Bosnian Serbs had not intended to take Gorazde, and he also asserted to you today - and this is on page 2, lines 12 to 15 - that there was no intention to take Gorazde and said that that was confirmed by that conversation of mine that Mladic recorded in his diary that we'd taken more than we had intended to and that our objective was that -- was to make it impossible for attacks from Gorazde. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, at the time of writing your book you had no access to a number of the documents you reviewed prior to giving evidence here, did you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And therefore, you had no information about any of the intentions as reflected in those documents?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: None at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter 08224, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is a document, General, from the VRS Main Staff to the Herzegovina Corps and the command of the Visegrad Tactical Group, and it's dated from 12 April 1994. And it notes that the president believes, as of the next day, 13 April, that they'd have three days to resolve the issue of Gorazde before a cessation of hostilities would be signed. In the last paragraph it's noted that the president insists and orders that the maximum use be made of this intervening period and that as much as possible be done in the sector of Gorazde in the given conditions. Let me know when you've had a chance to look --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this document appear to reflect information that you didn't have at the time of writing your book as regards the objective of the attack on Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly when I wrote the book I didn't have the benefit of having seen this document and the interpretation I put upon it is that the Bosnian Serb side wanted to maximise their military advantage in the intervening three days that they felt that they had.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And from this document do you infer anything as regards the effective control of the president?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I guess it was absolute.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have that as the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may state something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, not at this time. In relation to this document, Mr. Karadzic? Yes, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not denying the document, but that document was at the witness's disposal, at the OTP's disposal during the examination-in-chief. I would like to be able to say a couple of sentences about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of course, but I also think that this document should have been and could have been presented to the witness during the examination-in-chief. That's why I think I should be able to discuss this document with the witness at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit this document, but I was wondering whether your last question was in the remit of re-direct. Let's move on. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1684, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, on the subject of convoys at page 7434, lines 9 to 22, Dr. Karadzic put to you that the main reasons why convoys were being delayed were misunderstandings of different types. And you replied that there was an undue bureaucratic level that was employed against the running of convoys. And I think you were asked similar questions and gave similar answers throughout the course of your testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In this regard, I wonder if we could see 65 ter 22978. General, this is a document entitled BH command movsit as of 232359 B August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you just pull back, please, a little bit on the document so the General can see this whole first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you seen documents like this before during the course of your work with UNPROFOR, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd certainly been shown documents like this when the blocking of convoys was being discussed and we were developing policies as to how to deal with it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder then if -- well, perhaps I could ask you this. So, do you recall who prepares these documents then?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this would have been done as a result of an amalgam of information that was coming in from both the UNHCR and from the military commands and probably being brought together by the Chief of Staff of Bosnian command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to take us then straight away over to the last page of this document, page 7. Point number 7 bears the heading: Summary of convoy requests for 24 August 1994. And I wonder if under point D you could have a look at the list of refusals given by the Bosnian Serb headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those remarks match very much the sort of bureaucratic obstructions that were placed in our way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could this be the next Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1685, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, at page 7457, line 18, to 7459, line 1, you were taken to a letter of Dr. Karadzic's to Mr. Akashi dated 23 March 1994, touching on the topic of the Tuzla airport. And in referring to this document, Dr. Karadzic put to you the proposition that the Bosnian Serbs were never opposed to humanitarian aid even in situations when they were exposed to danger. You were asked whether their fears were legitimate. And your response was that this was a position in theory, but in practice it was the Serb side that did most of the blocking of the aid convoys. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember making that remark.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have a view as to whether these restrictions, convoy restrictions, based on security concerns, articulated security concerns, on the part of the Bosnian Serbs were justified?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
